The text teaches: *"When the three qualities that assist the mind — alertness, mindfulness, and focused investigation — are vigorous and strong, alertness becomes the awareness of release (vijja-vimutti), mindfulness becomes intuitive understanding (ñana), and focused investigation becomes liberating insight (vipassana-ñana), the discernment that can stay fixed on knowing the truth of stress without permitting any sense of pleasure or displeasure for its object to arise."* Rather than running away from discomfort or trying to suppress it, the Thai Forest approach is to turn around and investigate suffering directly (*dukkha-sacca*). How does 'The Eye of Discernment: An Anthology from the Teachings' characterize the nature of consciousness and the knowing mind?

The text observes: *"All you can do is say that the mind arises and falls away, the mind doesn't rise or fall away; the mind is good, the mind is evil; the mind becomes annihilated, the mind doesn't become annihilated; the mind is a dhamma, the mind isn't a dhamma; the mind gains release, the mind doesn't gain release; the mind is nibbana, the mind isn't nibbana; the mind is sensory consciousness, the mind isn't sensory consciousness; the mind is the heart, the mind isn't the heart..."* Consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is not an independent 'soul' or enduring self; it arises in dependence on contact (*phassa*) and sense objects. The practice is to distinguish between the passing objects of awareness (thoughts, feelings, sensations) and the pure, unattached quality of 'the one who knows' (*poo roo*), resting in unconditioned peace.

The text reflects: *"It stays as it is — what we suppose as thiti-dhamma, free from the germs of defilement — our very own heart, i.e., the heart's primal nature."* This passage points directly to the heart of experiential practice: letting go of superficial concepts and tuning awareness to the immediate truth of the moment. By investigating experience with honesty and forbearance (*khanti*), we discover an unshakable inner refuge that remains undisturbed by the worldly winds.

By investigating experience with honesty and forbearance (*khanti*), we discover an unshakable inner refuge that remains undisturbed by the worldly winds.

In 'The Eye of Discernment: An Anthology from the Teachings', what insight is conveyed by the reflection on: 'Craft Heart When first became...'?

The text reflects: *"Craft of the Heart
When I first became aware of the conflicting views held by people who practice — and of how ill-informed they are — I felt inspired by their desire to learn the truth, but at the same time dismayed over their views: right mixed with wrong, some people saying that nibbana and the paths leading to it still exist, others maintaining that nibbana has passed away and can no longer be attained."* This passage points directly to the heart of experiential practice: letting go of superficial concepts and tuning awareness to the immediate truth of the moment. By investigating experience with honesty and forbearance (*khanti*), we discover an unshakable inner refuge that remains undisturbed by the worldly winds.
